$m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$ for every $s \in S$. - $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$ for every $s \in S$. A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then $m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so $m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]). The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset $P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*), satisfying: - **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds: $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$. - **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$. We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by $$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$ Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$.

Its **positive part** and **negative part** are $$f^+ := \max\{f,0\},\qquad f^- := \max\{-f,0\}.$$ Pointwise, both functions take values in $[0,+\infty]$, and one has $$f = f^+ - f^-,\qquad |f| = f^+ + f^-.$$

derivations.claim: AC is the declared assumption and yields Countable Choice, so the choice hypotheses of the classical-derivative lemma, the box-measure theorem, the measurability interfaces and the representative-independence lemma are in force while the truncation calculus holds under AC itself; since M>0 the cube satisfies -2M<0<2M, so it is nonempty (0 in Q), and no representative is selected in the proof.

For every real t the functions max{0,t} and min{M,max{0,t}} take the values 0 for t<=0, t for 0<t<M and M for t>=M; moreover max{-M,max{0,t}}=max{0,t} because max{0,t}>=0>-M, so the truncation T_M of the corollary satisfies T_M(max{0,t})=min{M,max{0,t}} for every t.

The coordinate function f(x)=x_1 is C^1 on Q with partials d_1f=1 and d_jf=0 for j>=2: for each a in Q and each index j the difference quotient of the line map is the constant (e_j)_1 on the punctured line, whose limit at 0 is (e_j)_1 by the epsilon-delta criterion, so d_jf(a)=(e_j)_1 exists and equals 1 for j=1 and 0 otherwise; f is the first coordinate projection, hence continuous, and the partials are constant, hence continuous, so every word of length at most 1 has an existing continuous iterated derivative. The page label j is canonical coordinate j-1, as explicitly reconciled in F8; thus n=1 uses canonical index zero.

Q is the open box with a_i=-2M, b_i=2M, hence open with lambda_n(Q)=(4M)^n<infinity; for x in Q the inequalities -2M<x_1<2M give |x_1|<2M, so f and its first partials are bounded on Q by 2M and 1; being continuous they are Borel and Lebesgue measurable under Countable Choice, hence their classes lie in L-infinity(Q) and, by the finite-measure inclusion, in L^p(Q) for every 1<=p<=infinity.
The clipped function w vanishes for x_1<=0, equals x_1 for 0<x_1<M, and equals M for x_1>=M; these are pointwise identities on all of R^n.

By the classical-derivative lemma with k=1 applied to the C^1 function f, the classical derivatives d^alpha f for |alpha|<=1 are locally integrable and are the weak derivatives D^alpha f, with D^0f=f; combined with the L^p membership of f and its first partials, the Sobolev definition yields [f] in W^{1,p}(Q;R) with D_1[f]=[1] and D_j[f]=[0] for j>=2, the classes of the constant functions 1 and 0.

The positive part u:=f^+ of the real class [f], represented by the continuous function max{0,x_1}, lies in W^{1,p}(Q) with D_j u=1_{f>0}D_j f a.e., that is D_1u=[1_{x_1>0}] and D_j u=[0] for j>=2 almost everywhere on Q.

Applying the truncation clause to the real class u with the same level M gives T_M u in W^{1,p}(Q) with D_j T_M u=1_{{|u|<M}}D_j u a.e.; the representative max{0,x_1} of u satisfies T_M(max{0,x_1})=min{M,max{0,x_1}}=w pointwise, and w is measurable as the composition of the measurable positive part with the continuous map t->min{M,max{-M,t}}, so w is a representative of T_M u and [w]=T_M u lies in W^{1,p}(Q) for every 1<=p<=infinity.

On Q the level set is {|u|<M}={x_1<M}, so multiplying the representatives of step 4.1 gives 1_{x_1<M}1_{x_1>0}=1_{0<x_1<M} and 1_{x_1<M}*0=0 pointwise, the indicators being measurable and products of measurable functions measurable; hence D_1[w]=[1_{0<x_1<M}] and D_j[w]=[0] for j>=2 almost everywhere, that is, the weak gradient is e_1 on the middle slab and 0 for x_1<=0 and for x_1>=M. Threshold indicators are Borel measurable, not continuous: their fibers are Borel threshold sets and complements.

The interface pieces Q intersected with {x_1=0} and with {x_1=M} are boxes with a degenerate side, hence Lebesgue-null; by representative independence, modifying a locally integrable representative on a null set preserves the weak-derivative relation and the L^p class, so any function agreeing with 1_{0<x_1<M} off the two interface hyperplanes represents D_1[w], and any function agreeing with 0 off them represents D_j[w] for j>=2: interface values are irrelevant. Each interface lies between the empty open degenerate box and its closed box, so F13 applies to the actual mixed-face box.

Degenerate cases and accounting: n=1 is included since no step uses more than one coordinate direction; the exponent endpoints p=1 and p=infinity are included through steps 2.1 and 3.1 and the range of the truncation calculus; the level M>0 is fixed so Q has side 4M>0 and no limiting case M->0 or M=infinity is claimed; the only choice principle used is AC, through Countable Choice for the classical-derivative, measure, measurability and representative-independence interfaces and directly as the hypothesis of the truncation calculus, with no representative selected and no Dependent Choice invoked.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 proves the cube is nonempty (0 in Q since M>0 gives -2M<0<2M), so this example has no empty-domain case; the statement is about the fixed nonempty cube Q.
The zero region is treated in steps 2.2 and 6.1: w=0 on {x_1<=0} and its weak gradient is the zero class there, and no level M=0 is claimed because the statement fixes M>0.
Step 8.1 records that n=1 is included: no step uses more than one coordinate direction, and e_1 is then the single standard basis vector.

Step 7.1 treats the degenerate interface pieces {x_1=0} and {x_1=M}: they are boxes with a zero-length side, hence Lebesgue-null, so the gradient class is unaffected by interface values; the degenerate box case is exactly where the interface irrelevance is proved.

The exponent endpoints p=1 and p=infinity are handled in step 2.1 (L-infinity membership and the finite-measure inclusion cover every 1<=p<=infinity) and step 8.1 declares them included; the truncation calculus is stated for every 1<=p<=infinity.

Step 1.1 derives Countable Choice from AC and step 8.1 accounts for the uses: Countable Choice for the classical-derivative, box-measure, measurability and representative-independence interfaces, and AC itself as the hypothesis of the truncation calculus; no representative is selected.

boundaries.reason: The Statement contains no if-and-only-if claim: clause 1 is a membership assertion, clause 2 collects pointwise identities proved in step 2.2, and clause 3 identifies the gradient class through the almost-everywhere formulas of steps 6.1 and 7.1, so there is no forward implication of an equivalence to discharge.

Dually, there is no converse implication: the only equivalence-shaped content is the agreement of the two indicator conventions for the truncation, which the almost-everywhere statement of step 6.1 already absorbs, and the statement never claims that a function with the displayed gradient must be this particular clipping.
